studies.Title: Vegetable and fruit consumption and prostate cancer risk: a cohort study in The Netherlands.
studies.Reference: Vegetable and fruit consumption and prostate cancer risk: a cohort study in The Netherlands.
studies.Journal: Cancer epidemiology, biomarkers & prevention : a publication of the American Association for Cancer Research, cosponsored by the American Society of Preventive Oncology

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: The association between 21 vegetables and eight fruits and prostate cancer risk was assessed in the Netherlands Cohort Study among 58,279 men of ages 55-69 years at baseline in 1986. After 6.3 years of follow-up, 610 cases with complete vegetable data and 642 cases with complete fruit data were available for analysis.
extraction_supporting_text.cases: After 6.3 years of follow-up, 610 cases with complete vegetable data and 642 cases with complete fruit data were available for analysis.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: For vegetables categorized in botanical groups, no associations were found except for consumption of pulses (RR, 0.71; CI, 0.51-0.98; P for trend, 0.01).
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: In multivariate case-cohort analyses, the following rate ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for vegetable consumption were found (comparing highest versus lowest quintile): total vegetables (RR, 0.80; CI, 0.57-1.12); prepared vegetables (RR, 0.85; CI, 0.61-1.19); and raw vegetables (RR, 0.96; CI, 0.69-1.34). For vegetables categorized in botanical groups, no associations were found except for consumption of pulses (RR, 0.71; CI, 0.51-0.98; P for trend, 0.01).

extraction_supporting_text.design: assessed in the Netherlands Cohort Study
extraction_supporting_text.timing: at baseline in 1986. After 6.3 years of follow-up

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 6 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.77–0.95), suggesting that legumes is associated with a lower risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 53.84%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
